options: A reward model that trains too quickly and underfits
A policy, optimized via RL against a fixed and imperfect reward model, exploiting that model's blind spots so that proxy reward keeps rising while true human-judged quality stalls or falls
A bug where the reward model's weights are updated too many times per batch
A dataset collection error where chosen and rejected labels are swapped
questions.explain: Because the reward model is a fixed, imperfect proxy, continued RL optimization pressure eventually finds and exploits the gap between the proxy's score and real human preference.

questions.q: How does Goodhart's law apply to reward model overoptimization?
options: It states that reward models should never be used for RL
It states that once a measure (the reward model) becomes an explicit optimization target, it stops being a reliable measure of what it was meant to track
It is unrelated and only applies to economics
It states that RL always converges to the true optimum regardless of the reward function
questions.explain: Goodhart's law — "when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure" — describes exactly why hard-optimizing against the reward model breaks its correlation with real quality.

questions.q: What is a commonly observed concrete symptom of reward model overoptimization in practice?
options: The policy stops generating any text at all
A length bias, where the policy learns to pad responses to be longer and more hedging because the reward model subtly favors that, even though it reads as worse to humans
The reward model's loss increases to infinity
The tokenizer vocabulary shrinks
questions.explain: Reward models often have a bias toward verbosity; an RL-trained policy can learn to exploit that bias, inflating its proxy score without actually improving (and sometimes while harming) real quality.

questions.q: What pattern, plotted against RL training steps, is the telltale sign of overoptimization?
options: Both proxy reward and true quality fall together immediately
Proxy reward keeps climbing steadily while true quality rises, then plateaus, then falls — a widening gap between the two
Proxy reward and true quality are always identical by construction
Neither proxy reward nor true quality ever changes
questions.explain: The characteristic signature of overoptimization is a widening divergence: the proxy metric keeps improving while an independent measure of true quality stalls and then degrades.

questions.q: What does the KL penalty term, reward_used_for_RL = r_θ(x,y) − β·KL(π_RL || π_ref), do to help mitigate overoptimization?
options: It increases the reward model's accuracy on held-out data
It penalizes the RL policy for drifting too far from a fixed reference policy, limiting how far it can wander in search of reward-model blind spots
It retrains the reward model from scratch at every RL step
It removes the need for a Bradley-Terry loss entirely
questions.explain: The KL term grows as the RL policy's output distribution diverges from the reference policy, discouraging the large distributional shifts typically needed to find and exploit rare reward-model errors.
